claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations described in the text and shown in figures.

claims.claim: Biofilms formed by C. parapsilosis have a layer of filamentous cells composed largely of pseudohyphae rather than a mixture of true hyphae and pseudohyphae.
claims.source: Biofilms formed by C. parapsilosis appeared similar at low resolution, but a closer examination showed that the layer of filamentous cells is composed largely of pseudohyphae rather than a mixture of true hyphae and pseudohyphae (Figure 2B).

claims.claim: L. elongisporus formed thinner biofilms composed only of yeast cells under the tested conditions.

claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations described in the text.

claims.claim: S. passalidarum, M. guilliermondii, and C. lusitaniae form even thinner biofilms than L. elongisporus.
claims.source: Moving further away from C. albicans, Spathaspora passalidarum, Meyerozyma guilliermondii, and Clavispora lusitaniae form even thinner biofilms, while Scheffersomyces stipites, Debaryomyces hansenii, Metschnikowia bicuspidate, Hyphopichia burtonii, and Candida tenuis did not form biofilms under the conditions we tested; only a few cells were observed adhering to the surface (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: S. stipites, D. hansenii, M. bicuspidate, H. burtonii, and C. tenuis did not form biofilms under the conditions tested; only a few cells were observed adhering to the surface.
claims.source: Moving further away from C. albicans, Spathaspora passalidarum, Meyerozyma guilliermondii, and Clavispora lusitaniae form even thinner biofilms, while Scheffersomyces stipites, Debaryomyces hansenii, Metschnikowia bicuspidate, Hyphopichia burtonii, and Candida tenuis did not form biofilms under the conditions we tested; only a few cells were observed adhering to the surface (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: C. glabrata and S. cerevisiae did not form biofilms that resembled those formed by C. albicans and its close relatives in the assays and conditions tested.
claims.source: As can be seen in Figure 2, neither of these species formed biofilms that resembled those formed by C. albicans and its close relatives in the assays and conditions that we tested.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: All four species (C. albicans, C. dubliniensis, C. tropicalis, and C. parapsilosis) were able to form biofilms in the rat catheter model.
claims.source: All four species were able to form biofilms, although the biofilms formed by C. albicans and C. dubliniensis were considerably thicker and more filamentous (Figure 2C).

claims.claim: The biofilms formed by C. albicans and C. dubliniensis in the rat catheter model were considerably thicker and more filamentous than those formed by C. tropicalis and C. parapsilosis.
claims.source: All four species were able to form biofilms, although the biofilms formed by C. albicans and C. dubliniensis were considerably thicker and more filamentous (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: C. albicans biofilm formation is the most rapid and most robust to environmental changes as it formed similar biofilms in all media tested.
claims.source: Of all the species studied, C. albicans biofilm formation is the most rapid and most robust to environmental changes as it formed similar biofilms in all media tested (Supplementary file 1a, Figure 2—figure supplement 2); moreover, the biofilms formed by this species are the most stable to physical manipulation (results not shown).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental data presented in Supplementary file 1a and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The biofilms formed by C. albicans are the most stable to physical manipulation.
claims.source: Of all the species studied, C. albicans biofilm formation is the most rapid and most robust to environmental changes as it formed similar biofilms in all media tested (Supplementary file 1a, Figure 2—figure supplement 2); moreover, the biofilms formed by this species are the most stable to physical manipulation (results not shown).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text but the supporting data is not shown.

claims.claim: All seven master regulators of the C. albicans biofilm network have clear orthologs in C. dubliniensis, C. tropicalis, and C. parapsilosis, with the exception of Rob1.
claims.source: All seven master regulators of the network in C. albicans (Figure 1) have clear orthologs in the other three closely related species, with the exception of Rob1.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claims.claim: Rob1 has a patchy phylogenetic distribution, with syntenic orthologs present in C. albicans, C. dubliniensis, and C. tropicalis, but apparently absent from C. parapsilosis and closely related species.
claims.source: Rob1 has a patchy phylogenetic distribution, with syntenic orthologs present in C. albicans, C. dubiniensis, and C. tropicalis, but apparently absent from C. parapsilosis and closely related species.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claims.claim: Rob1 orthologs are present in other more distantly related CTG species, which supports the hypothesis that Rob1 was either lost or was evolving sufficiently rapidly in the C. parapsilosis lineage that it cannot be recognized.
claims.source: However, Rob1 orthologs are present in other more distantly related CTG species, which supports the hypothesis that Rob1 was either lost or was evolving sufficiently rapidly in the C. parapsilosis lineage that it cannot be recognized (Maguire et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Maguire et al., 2013).

claims.claim: All seven master regulators identified in C. albicans were also required for biofilm formation in C. dubliniensis.
claims.source: As can be observed in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, all seven master regulators identified in C. albicans were also required for biofilm formation in C. dubliniensis.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Only five of the seven master regulators (not Rob1 and Flo8) were required for biofilm formation in C. tropicalis.
claims.source: The results were different for C. tropicalis; here, only five of the seven were required, with Rob1 and Flo8 appearing dispensable for biofilm formation under our laboratory conditions.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental data described in the text and shown in figures.

claims.claim: The biofilms formed by the rob1 and flo8 deletion mutants in C. tropicalis were actually slightly heavier and the hyphal layer was denser than biofilms formed by the parental (wildtype) strain.
claims.source: The biofilms formed by the rob1 and flo8 deletion mutants in C. tropicalis were actually slightly heavier and the hyphal layer was denser than biofilms formed by the parental (wildtype) strain, suggesting that these two regulators may have assumed a subtle inhibitory role in this species.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations described in the text.

claims.claim: Rob1 and Flo8 may have assumed a subtle inhibitory role in biofilm formation in C. tropicalis.
claims.source: The biofilms formed by the rob1 and flo8 deletion mutants in C. tropicalis were actually slightly heavier and the hyphal layer was denser than biofilms formed by the parental (wildtype) strain, suggesting that these two regulators may have assumed a subtle inhibitory role in this species.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observation that deletion mutants form thicker biofilms.

claims.claim: For C. parapsilosis, only Bcr1 and Efg1 are indispensable for biofilm formation among the seven master biofilm regulators in C. albicans.
claims.source: For C. parapsilosis, it was previously shown that, of the seven master biofilm regulators in C. albicans, only Bcr1 and Efg1 are indispensable for biofilm formation.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on prior work as indicated by the phrase 'it was previously shown'.

claims.claim: The Ndt80 deletion in C. parapsilosis fails to form biofilms but also has a general growth defect, making it difficult to ascertain its precise role.
claims.source: The Ntd80 deletion in C. parapsilosis fails to form biofilms but also has a general growth defect, making it difficult to ascertain its precise role.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claims.claim: Deletion of CZF1, UME6, CPH2, GZF3, and ACE2 all exhibit biofilm-specific defects in C. parapsilosis but not in C. albicans.
claims.source: Previous work also established that deletion of CZF1, UME6, CPH2, GZF3, and ACE2 all exhibit biofilm-specific defects in C. parapsilosis but not in C. albicans (Holland et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Holland et al., 2014).

claims.claim: The group of master regulators underlying biofilm formation in C. albicans is different than in other Candida species with the degree of difference roughly paralleling their evolutionary distance from C. albicans.
claims.source: Overall, our results, together with previous observations, show that the group of master regulators underlying biofilm formation in C. albicans is different than in other Candida species with the degree of difference roughly paralleling their evolutionary distance from C. albicans.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript and prior work.

claims.claim: The connections between master regulators and conserved target genes vary greatly across Candida species.
claims.source: If we consider only the one-to-one orthologs, it becomes clear that the connections between master regulators and conserved target genes vary greatly across these species (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Between C. albicans and C. dubliniensis, the master regulator that showed the highest conservation of target gene connections was Ndt80, but the overlap was only about 50% (634 of 1,297).
claims.source: Between the two most closely related species (C. albicans and C. dubliniensis), the master regulator that showed the highest conservation of target gene connections was Ndt80, but the overlap was only about 50% (634 of 1,297).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: Between C. albicans and C. parapsilosis, the overlap of Ndt80 target gene connections drops to about 26% (722 of 2,725).
claims.source: Between C. albicans and C. parapsilosis, this value drops to about 26% (722 of 2,725).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: Only 12% (371 of 3,016) of Ndt80 target gene connections are common to all four species (C. albicans, C. dubliniensis, C. tropicalis, and C. parapsilosis).
claims.source: Although only 12% (371 of 3,016) of Ndt80 target gene connections are common to all four species, the overlap for each species pair is larger than expected by chance (hypergeometric test, p<0.05).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data analysis and statistical testing.

claims.claim: The overlap of Ndt80 target gene connections for each species pair is larger than expected by chance (hypergeometric test, p<0.05).
claims.source: Although only 12% (371 of 3,016) of Ndt80 target gene connections are common to all four species, the overlap for each species pair is larger than expected by chance (hypergeometric test, p<0.05).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on statistical testing of ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: Rob1 shares only about 12% (2 of 17) of its target gene connections between C. albicans and C. dubliniensis, but the overlap is still greater than expected by chance (hypergeometric test, p<0.05).
claims.source: For example, Rob1 shares only about 12% (2 of 17) of its target gene connections between the two most related species, C. albicans and C. dubliniensis, but the overlap is still greater than expected by chance (hypergeometric test, p<0.05).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data analysis and statistical testing.

claims.claim: Each species has target genes in its biofilm network that lack orthologs in the other three species.
claims.source: Our results also show that each species has target genes in its biofilm network that lack orthologs in the other three species.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of ChIP-seq data and ortholog identification.

claims.claim: In C. albicans, 26% of the genes bound by at least one of the biofilm master regulators do not have orthologs in the other three species compared with 19% for the genome as a whole.
claims.source: In C. albicans, 26% of the genes bound by at least one of the biofilm master regulators do not have orthologs in the other three species compared with 19% for the genome as a whole.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of ChIP-seq data and ortholog identification.

claims.claim: Genes that are upregulated during biofilm formation in C. albicans are often 'young' genes, that is, genes that lack orthologs in related species.
claims.source: This analysis extends the previous observation that genes that are upregulated during biofilm formation in C. albicans are often 'young' genes, that is, genes that lack orthologs in related species (Nobile et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Nobile et al., 2012) and extended by the current analysis.

claims.claim: A similar enrichment of unique genes in the biofilm network was observed in C. parapsilosis, but not for C. dubliniensis and C. tropicalis.
claims.source: We observed a similar enrichment of unique genes in the biofilm network of C. parapsilosis, but not for C. dubliniensis and C. tropicalis; in the latter two species, the fraction of non-orthologous genes in the biofilm network was approximately the same as that observed for the whole genome.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of ChIP-seq data and ortholog identification.

claims.claim: The biofilm networks of C. albicans and C. parapsilosis have been more dynamic in recent evolutionary time than those of C. dubliniensis and C. tropicalis.
claims.source: These observations indicate that the biofilm networks of C. albicans and C. parapsilosis have been more dynamic in recent evolutionary time than those of the other two species.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that C. albicans and C. parapsilosis have more unique genes in their biofilm networks.

claims.claim: The binding motif for some of the master regulators does not vary significantly across the species studied.
claims.source: As discussed below, the binding motif for some of the master regulators does not vary significantly across the species we studied.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on de novo motif analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: The high proportion of differences in regulator-target gene connections across Candida species did not significantly change when the stringency of the filtering criteria increased.
claims.source: Although the gross number of regulator-target gene connections decreased as the stringency of the filtering criteria increased, the high proportion of differences across Candida species described above did not significantly change (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of ChIP-seq data with different filtering criteria, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The binding intensities of Ndt80 in all the intergenic regions of the genome were highly correlated between the two media tested (Spider 1% glucose and alternative media) in C. albicans, C. dubliniensis, and C. tropicalis.
claims.source: In all species, the binding intensities of the regulator in all the intergenic regions of the genome were highly correlated between the two media tested (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: There are no significant changes in Ndt80 binding when the growth media is modified.
claims.source: This finding indicates that there are no significant changes in Ndt80 binding when the growth media is modified.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the high correlation of binding intensities between different media.

claims.claim: Many target genes were directly connected (by binding) to more than one master regulator in C. albicans.
claims.source: The initial characterization of the biofilm transcription circuit in C. albicans showed that many target genes were directly connected (by binding) to more than one master regulator (Nobile et al., 2012), and this general feature of the network architecture is observed across the Candida species studied here, despite the low conservation of individual regulator-target gene connections (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Nobile et al., 2012) and extended by the current analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: High connectivity of the biofilm network is observed across the Candida species studied, despite the low conservation of individual regulator-target gene connections.
claims.source: The initial characterization of the biofilm transcription circuit in C. albicans showed that many target genes were directly connected (by binding) to more than one master regulator (Nobile et al., 2012), and this general feature of the network architecture is observed across the Candida species studied here, despite the low conservation of individual regulator-target gene connections (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Over 75% of the Efg1 target genes are also Ndt80 targets in all four species.
claims.source: The set of target genes of Ndt80 is considerably larger, but over 75% of the Efg1 target genes are also Ndt80 targets in all four species.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: The binding motifs of Ndt80 and Efg1 are enriched in each other's binding locations in all four species studied.
claims.source: In addition, the binding motifs of these two regulators are enriched in each other's binding locations in all four species studied (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on motif analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: In all species, Efg1 binds in conjunction with Ndt80 even though the target genes of the regulator combination differ greatly across species.
claims.source: These observations indicate that, in all species, Efg1 binds in conjunction with Ndt80 even though the target genes of the regulator combination differ greatly across species.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that Efg1 and Ndt80 binding motifs are enriched in each other's binding locations.

claims.claim: The association between Efg1 and Ndt80 agrees with previous planktonic ChIP-seq experiments of Efg1 performed in C. parapsilosis where the most enriched binding motif found was that of Ndt80.
claims.source: The association between Efg1 and Ndt80 agrees with previous planktonic ChIP-seq experiments of Efg1 performed in C. parapsilosis where the most enriched binding motif found was that of Ndt80 (Connolly et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Connolly et al., 2013).

claims.claim: The DNA-binding motifs of Efg1 and Ndt80 have been shown to co-occur in the binding regions of Sfl1 and Sfl2, two regulators of filamentation in C. albicans.
claims.source: The DNA-binding motifs of these two regulators have also been shown to co-occur in the binding regions of Sfl1 and Sfl2, two regulators of filamentation in C. albicans (Znaidi et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Znaidi et al., 2013).

claims.claim: The Efg1-Ndt80 association is ancient with respect to the Candida species studied and remains preserved across them despite large species-to-species differences in the target genes bound by the two regulators.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggest that the Efg1-Ndt80 association is ancient with respect to the Candida species studied here and that it remains preserved across them despite large species-to-species differences in the target genes bound by the two regulators.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that Efg1 and Ndt80 binding motifs co-occur across species and in prior work.

claims.claim: Combinational control of target genes is very common in all species.
claims.source: Analysis of the other master regulators indicates that combinational control of target genes is very common in all species, although the other examples do not seem as deeply conserved as the Efg1-Ndt8o example.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of ChIP-seq data for multiple regulators.

claims.claim: Ndt80 shows the highest conservation of binding connections between one master regulator and the others.
claims.source: The extent of conservation of the binding connections between one master regulator and the others varies from regulator to regulator (Supplementary file 1c), with Ndt80 showing the highest conservation.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of ChIP-seq data presented in Supplementary file 1c.

claims.claim: In all four species, Ndt80 binds to its own control region as well as those of all six other regulators, with the exception of the control region of FLO8 in C. albicans and ROB1 in C. dubliniensis.
claims.source: In all four species, Ndt80 binds to its own control region as well as those of all six other regulators, with the exception of the control region of FLO8 in C. albicans and ROB1 in C. dubliniensis.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: Ndt80 and Efg1 each bind to their own control regions in all four species analyzed.
claims.source: Ndt80 and Efg1 each bind to their own control regions in all the four species analyzed, while Brg1 exhibits this interaction only in C. albicans and C. dubliniensis.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: Brg1 binds to its own control region only in C. albicans and C. dubliniensis.
claims.source: Ndt80 and Efg1 each bind to their own control regions in all the four species analyzed, while Brg1 exhibits this interaction only in C. albicans and C. dubliniensis.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: High connectivity between the master regulators is conserved in the four Candida species analyzed.
claims.source: Overall, our findings show that high connectivity between the master regulators is conserved in the four Candida species analyzed.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: Despite the extensive changes in the network across species, the high connectivity among regulators remains a structural feature of the network in each species.
claims.source: Thus, despite the extensive changes in the network across species, the high connectivity among regulators remains a structural feature of the network in each species.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that high connectivity is conserved despite changes in individual connections.

claims.claim: The enriched DNA-binding motifs found in the binding regions of the biofilm master regulators were very similar across the four species examined.
claims.source: Performing de novo motif searches, we found that the enriched DNA-binding motifs found in the binding regions of the biofilm master regulators were very similar across the four species we examined (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on de novo motif analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The de novo generated DNA-binding motifs for Efg1 and Ndt80 are similar to those previously reported for their orthologs in C. albicans and other species.
claims.source: Moreover, the de novo generated DNA-binding motifs for Efg1 and Ndt80 are similar to those previously reported for their orthologs in C. albicans and other species (Nobile et al., 2012; Nocedal et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Nobile et al., 2012; Nocedal et al., 2017).

claims.claim: The overlap of potential targets between species based on motif scoring varied from 51 to 100% depending on the exact motif used, but was never low enough to account for the differences determined directly from the ChIP-seq experiments.
claims.source: The overlap of potential targets between species varied from 51 to 100% depending on the exact motif used, but was never low enough to account for the differences determined directly from the ChIP-seq experiments (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on motif analysis and comparison with ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: The large differences in regulator-target interactions across species observed in the ChIP-seq data cannot be accounted for by slight differences in the binding motifs generated in each individual species.
claims.source: In other words, the large differences in regulator-target interactions across species observed in the ChIP-seq data cannot be accounted for by slight differences in the binding motifs generated in each individual species.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that motif-based predictions do not explain the observed differences in ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: The DNA-binding specificity of at least some of the master regulators has not changed significantly across these species.
claims.source: Although we cannot fully disregard that small differences in binding affinity contribute to differences in master regulator-target gene connections observed across the species, overall, all the analyses show that the DNA-binding specificity of at least some of the master regulators has not changed significantly across these species.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on motif analysis and ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: The pairwise differences in the transcription profiles across the three species (C. albicans, C. dubliniensis, and C. tropicalis) are significant and reflect their phylogenetic position: the further apart the two species are from one another, the less correlated their transcription profiles are.
claims.source: As seen in Figure 5B, the pairwise differences in the transcription profiles across the three species are significant and reflect their phylogenetic position: the further apart the two species are from one another, the less correlated their transcription profiles are.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on transcription profiling data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Only 29% of the genes that change their expression during biofilm formation are shared between C. albicans and C. dubliniensis (using a twofold cutoff).

For example, only 29% of the genes that change their expression during biofilm formation are shared between C. albicans and C. dubliniensis, and only 24% are shared between C. albicans and C. tropicalis.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on transcription profiling data analysis.

claims.claim: Only 24% of the genes that change their expression during biofilm formation are shared between C. albicans and C. tropicalis (using a twofold cutoff).
claims.source: If we use a lax cutoff of twofold over/underexpression to define genes that change their expression during biofilm formation, the overlap between pairs of species is relatively low. For example, only 29% of the genes that change their expression during biofilm formation are shared between C. albicans and C. dubliniensis, and only 24% are shared between C. albicans and C. tropicalis.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on transcription profiling data analysis.

claims.claim: The overlap of differentially expressed genes between the two C. albicans isolates was 48%.
claims.source: The overlap of differentially expressed genes between the two C. albicans isolates was 48%.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on transcription profiling data analysis.

claims.claim: Clinical isolates differ in their biofilm-forming abilities.
claims.source: This result is consistent with previous work showing that clinical isolates differ in their biofilm-forming abilities (Hirakawa et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Hirakawa et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2019).

claims.claim: All the interspecific pairwise overlaps of differentially expressed genes are greater than would be expected by chance (hypergeometric test, p<<0.05).
claims.source: Despite these major differences, all the interspecific pairwise overlaps are greater than would be expected by chance (hypergeometric test, p<<0.05), although we cannot distinguish if this is due primarily to selection or to the shared ancestry of their promoter sequences.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on statistical testing of transcription profiling data.

claims.claim: The low degree of conservation in genome-wide gene expression agrees well with the low conservation of regulator-target gene connections across species.
claims.source: Overall, the low degree of conservation in genome-wide gene expression agrees well with the low conservation of regulator-target gene connections across species described above.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the comparison of gene expression and ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: The fraction of differentially expressed genes bound by one or more regulators ranges from 30% in C. albicans to 51% in C. tropicalis.

claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of ChIP-seq and transcription profiling data.

claims.claim: 67% of differently expressed genes in C. parapsilosis were bound by at least one of the biofilm regulators under the experimental conditions tested.
claims.source: Combining our data with previous transcriptional profiling experiments performed in C. parapsilosis during biofilm formation (Holland et al., 2014), we estimated that 67% of differently expressed genes in this species were bound by at least one of the biofilm regulators under the experimental conditions tested.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of ChIP-seq data and prior transcription profiling data (Holland et al., 2014).

claims.claim: The overlap between differential gene expression and regulator binding in all species is larger than what would be expected by chance (hypergeometric test, p<<0.05), suggesting that direct binding is an important factor in gene regulation in the biofilm network.
claims.source: The overlap between differential gene expression and regulator binding in all species is larger than what would be expected by chance (hypergeometric test, p<<0.05), suggesting that direct binding is an important factor in gene regulation in the biofilm network.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on statistical testing of ChIP-seq and transcription profiling data.

claims.claim: Most genes that are expressed differentially between species are genes whose intergenic region is bound by at least one regulator in one species, but not in the other species.
claims.source: Pairwise comparisons of C. albicans, C. dubliniensis, and C. tropicalis showed that most genes that are expressed differentially between species (as defined above) are genes whose intergenic region is bound by at least one regulator in one species, but not in the other species.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of ChIP-seq and transcription profiling data.

claims.claim: This association is statistically significant (Fisher's two-tailed exact test, p<<0.05) suggesting that the majority of differences in biofilm-specific gene expression between species can be explained by differences in the cis-regulatory sequences of target genes that alter binding of the regulators.

claims.evidence: The claim is based on statistical testing of ChIP-seq and transcription profiling data.

claims.claim: C. albicans and C. dubliniensis can be mated to generate tetraploid hybrids.
claims.source: We took advantage of the fact that it is possible to mate C. albicans and C. dubliniensis (each diploid) to generate tetraploid hybrids (Pujol et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Pujol et al., 2004).

claims.claim: C. albicans-C. dubliniensis hybrids form biofilms similar to those formed by C. albicans.
claims.source: These hybrids form biofilms similar to those formed by C. albicans (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In the C. albicans-C. dubliniensis hybrid, the target genes bound by the C. albicans Ndt80 and the C. dubliniensis Ndt80 were highly correlated, similar to two biological replicates carried out in the same species.
claims.source: The results showed that — in the hybrid — the target genes bound by the C. albicans Ndt80 and the C. dubliniensis Ndt80 were highly correlated, similar to two biological replicates carried out in the same species (Figure 6A).

claims.claim: In the hybrid, the same target genes were obtained regardless of which Ndt80 was tagged for immunoprecipitation.

results.result: The biofilm transcription network in C. albicans consists of seven master regulators (Bcr1, Brg1, Efg1, Flo8, Ndt80, Rob1, Tec1) that collectively bind to over a thousand target genes (~1/6 of the genome) and are all required for normal biofilm development.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 describe the C. albicans biofilm network based on prior work (Nobile et al., 2012; Fox et al., 2015) and Figure 1. These are well-established findings from the literature that provide the foundation for the current study.

results.result: Genes highly expressed during C. albicans biofilm formation are enriched for 'young' genes with orthologs only in closely related species. C. parapsilosis diverged ~70 million years ago and has orthologs for six of seven master regulators, but only two are required for biofilm formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C7 summarize prior findings (Nobile et al., 2012; Mishra et al., 2007; Butler et al., 2009; Holland et al., 2014) that motivate the current study. These establish the evolutionary context and prior knowledge about network divergence.

results.result: C. dubliniensis and C. tropicalis are more closely related to C. albicans than C. parapsilosis (divergence times ~20, 45, and 70 million years respectively), are known to form biofilms, but their regulatory circuits are largely unknown.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10, C13-C15 establish the phylogenetic relationships and prior knowledge about biofilm formation in these species, supported by multiple citations and Figure 2. This provides the rationale for studying these particular species.

results.result: Spider medium with 1% glucose allowed all four species (C. albicans, C. dubliniensis, C. tropicalis, C. parapsilosis) to form thick, well-structured biofilms by 48 hours, though C. albicans formed biofilms in all media tested while C. tropicalis was carbon source-dependent.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C19 describe the optimization of biofilm growth conditions, supported by experimental data in Supplementary file 1a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The 48-hour timepoint and Spider glucose medium were established as optimal for comparative studies.

results.result: Biofilm complexity correlates with phylogenetic distance from C. albicans: only C. dubliniensis and C. tropicalis form structurally similar biofilms with yeast and filamentous layers; C. parapsilosis forms biofilms with mostly pseudohyphae; more distant species form thinner biofilms or no biofilms.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C26 describe the phenotypic characterization of biofilms across 15 species, supported by data in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplements. The correlation between phylogenetic distance and biofilm complexity is clearly demonstrated through multiple assays (CSLM, biomass, microfluidics).

results.result: All four focal species form biofilms in the rat catheter model, with C. albicans and C. dubliniensis forming considerably thicker and more filamentous biofilms than C. tropicalis and C. parapsilosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C28 demonstrate that in vitro findings translate to an in vivo model, supported by data in Figure 2C. This validates the biological relevance of the in vitro observations.

results.result: C. albicans biofilm formation is the most rapid and robust to environmental changes, forming similar biofilms in all media tested, and the biofilms are the most stable to physical manipulation.
results.evaluation: Claim C29 is supported by data in Supplementary file 1a and Figure 2—figure supplement 2. However, C30 states that supporting data for physical stability is 'not shown', making this claim impossible to verify from the presented evidence.

results.result: All seven C. albicans master regulators have clear orthologs in the other three species except Rob1, which has a patchy distribution (present in C. albicans, C. dubliniensis, C. tropicalis but absent from C. parapsilosis), likely due to loss or rapid evolution in the C. parapsilosis lineage.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C33 describe the ortholog distribution of master regulators, supported by citation to Maguire et al., 2013. The patchy distribution of Rob1 is explained by evolutionary inference based on its presence in more distant species.

results.result: The requirement for master regulators in biofilm formation varies by species: all seven are required in C. dubliniensis, five in C. tropicalis (Rob1 and Flo8 dispensable and possibly inhibitory), and only Bcr1 and Efg1 are indispensable in C. parapsilosis, with the degree of difference correlating with evolutionary distance from C. albicans.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C41 describe gene deletion experiments in C. dubliniensis and C. tropicalis (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and cite prior work for C. parapsilosis (Holland et al., 2014). The data clearly show species-specific requirements for master regulators, though C37 (inhibitory role) is speculative based on slightly increased biofilm mass.

results.result: Master regulator-target gene connections vary greatly across species: Ndt80 shows the highest conservation but only ~50% overlap between C. albicans and C. dubliniensis, dropping to ~26% with C. parapsilosis, with only 12% common to all four species. Rob1 shows even lower conservation (~12% between C. albicans and C. dubliniensis). All overlaps are statistically significant (p<0.05).
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C47 describe ChIP-seq analysis of regulator-target gene connections (Figure 4). The quantitative data clearly demonstrate low conservation of individual connections despite statistical significance, supported by hypergeometric tests. This is a central finding of the manuscript.

results.result: Each species has target genes in its biofilm network lacking orthologs in other species. In C. albicans, 26% of genes bound by master regulators lack orthologs (vs 19% genome-wide), extending prior observations about 'young' genes. Similar enrichment occurs in C. parapsilosis but not C. dubliniensis or C. tropicalis, indicating more dynamic recent evolution in C. albicans and C. parapsilosis networks.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 describe ortholog analysis of target genes, extending prior work (Nobile et al., 2012). The enrichment of species-specific genes in biofilm networks of C. albicans and C. parapsilosis is clearly demonstrated, though the inference about 'dynamic evolution' (C52) is interpretive.

results.result: The binding motifs for some master regulators do not vary significantly across species, and the high proportion of differences in regulator-target connections remains unchanged with increased stringency of filtering criteria or different growth media.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 address potential technical concerns about the ChIP-seq analysis. The robustness of findings to different filtering criteria (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and growth media (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) strengthens the conclusion that observed differences are real.

results.result: High connectivity of the biofilm network (many target genes bound by multiple regulators) is conserved across species despite low conservation of individual connections. Over 75% of Efg1 targets are also Ndt80 targets in all species, with their binding motifs enriched in each other's locations. This ancient Efg1-Ndt80 association is preserved across species despite different target genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C64 describe network architecture analysis from ChIP-seq data (Figure 4A, Figure 5A). The conservation of high connectivity and the Efg1-Ndt80 association is well-supported by data and consistent with prior work (Nobile et al., 2012; Connolly et al., 2013; Znaidi et al., 2013). This is a key finding about preserved network structure.

results.result: Combinatorial control of target genes is common in all species. Ndt80 shows the highest conservation of connections to other master regulators, binding to its own control region and those of all six other regulators (with minor exceptions) in all species. High connectivity among regulators is conserved despite extensive network changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C71 describe the regulatory connections among master regulators based on ChIP-seq data (Supplementary file 1c). The conservation of high connectivity and autoregulation despite changes in individual connections is clearly demonstrated and represents an important structural feature of network evolution.

results.result: DNA-binding motifs of master regulators are very similar across species and match previously reported motifs. Motif-based predictions of target overlap (51-100%) cannot account for the low overlap observed in ChIP-seq experiments, indicating that DNA-binding specificity has not changed significantly and differences are due to cis-regulatory changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C76 describe de novo motif analysis (Figure 5) and comparison with ChIP-seq data. The conservation of binding motifs despite divergent target genes strongly supports the conclusion that cis-regulatory changes, not trans changes in regulator specificity, drive network evolution. This is a critical mechanistic finding.

results.result: Biofilm-specific gene expression differs considerably across species, correlating with phylogenetic distance. Only 29% of differentially expressed genes are shared between C. albicans and C. dubliniensis, and 24% between C. albicans and C. tropicalis. Even between two C. albicans isolates, overlap is only 48%. All interspecific overlaps are greater than expected by chance (p<<0.05).
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C83 describe transcription profiling results (Figure 5B). The low conservation of gene expression changes is consistent with the low conservation of regulator-target connections. The comparison with C. albicans isolates (C80-C81) provides important context, though the inference about recent mutations (C81) relies on prior work.

results.result: 30-67% of differentially expressed genes during biofilm formation are bound by at least one master regulator, significantly more than expected by chance (p<<0.05). Most genes differentially expressed between species have differential regulator binding, suggesting that differences in biofilm-specific gene expression are explained by cis-regulatory changes affecting regulator binding (Fisher's test, p<<0.05).
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C88 integrate ChIP-seq and expression data to link regulator binding to gene expression changes. The statistical analyses support the conclusion that cis-regulatory changes drive expression divergence. This provides mechanistic insight into how network changes affect phenotype.

results.result: In C. albicans-C. dubliniensis tetraploid hybrids, Ndt80 from either species binds the same target genes, with binding positions on each genome characteristic of that species (96-97% match). This confirms that differences in regulator-target connections are due to cis-regulatory changes rather than trans changes in regulators or physiological differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C95 describe the hybrid experiment (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), which provides independent validation of the cis-regulatory hypothesis. The high correlation of binding regardless of which Ndt80 is tagged, combined with genome-specific binding patterns, strongly supports the conclusion. This is a critical validation experiment.

results.result: As phylogenetic distance from C. albicans increases, biofilms become less complex and fewer master regulators are required: all seven in C. dubliniensis, five in C. tropicalis (Rob1 and Flo8 dispensable), and only Bcr1 and Efg1 indispensable in C. parapsilosis (where other regulators have assumed master roles). At larger distances, species do not form biofilms.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C102 summarize the main findings about phenotypic and regulatory evolution. These are well-supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript (Figures 2-3) and prior work (Holland et al., 2014). This represents a major conclusion of the study.

results.result: Differences in regulator-target gene connections across species are due largely to changes in cis-regulatory sequences rather than changes in the regulators themselves.
results.evaluation: Claim C105 restates the conclusion from the hybrid experiment (C95). This is strongly supported by the hybrid ChIP-seq data (Figure 6A) and motif conservation analysis (Figure 5), representing a central mechanistic finding of the study.

results.result: mRNA expression during biofilm formation differs considerably between species, with divergence increasing with phylogenetic distance.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C107 summarize the transcription profiling results (Figure 5B). This is well-supported by the data and represents a major finding about the functional consequences of network evolution.

results.result: Despite extensive changes in transcription networks, key architectural features are preserved: high connectivity (many target genes bound by multiple regulators, dominated by Ndt80 and Efg1), and self-regulation (regulators binding their own and other regulators' control regions). These structural features are likely common to many complex transcription networks.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C114 describe the conservation of network architecture despite changes in individual connections. This is well-supported by ChIP-seq data and represents a major conceptual finding. The generalization to other networks (C113) is supported by citation to prior work (Sorrells and Johnson, 2015).

results.result: Specific master regulator-target gene connections preserved across multiple species may point to target genes notably important for biofilm formation.
results.evaluation: Claim C115 is explicitly speculative ('may point to'), suggesting a hypothesis for future work. While reasonable, this cannot be evaluated as supported or unsupported without additional functional validation experiments.

results.result: Prior studies of C. albicans clinical isolates show variation in biofilm formation, with SC5314 (used in this study) among the thickest biofilm producers. One isolate with poor biofilm formation had an inactivating EFG1 mutation. SC5314 is a good representative of C. albicans as a species, with most clinical isolates likely acquiring mutations recently.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C121 discuss prior work (Hirakawa et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2019) to justify the choice of SC5314 as representative. The inference that SC5314 is representative (C119, C121) is based on comparison with C. dubliniensis CD36 biofilm phenotype, which is reasonable but somewhat indirect.

results.result: This is the first detailed examination of how a complex transcription network changes over relatively short evolutionary time (~70 million years) across four species.
results.evaluation: Claim C122 asserts the novelty of the study. While difficult to verify exhaustively, the comprehensive nature of the analysis (phenotypes, gene deletions, ChIP-seq for multiple regulators across four species, expression profiling, hybrid validation) does appear unprecedented in scope.

results.result: Although biofilms from different Candida species have similarities, they differ in subtle aspects. C. albicans biofilms form faster, under a greater range of conditions, and are more difficult to disrupt than C. dubliniensis biofilms, despite appearing similar under confocal microscopy.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C124 describe subtle phenotypic differences between closely related species, supported by experimental observations throughout the manuscript (Figures 2-3, Supplementary file 1a). These differences provide context for interpreting the molecular changes.

results.result: It is difficult to reconcile subtle phenotypic differences with large transcriptional circuitry differences. The authors propose that many changes result from neutral evolution (constructive neutral evolution), where molecular complexity can change without fitness increase.
results.evaluation: Claim C125 acknowledges a conceptual challenge. Claim C126 proposes neutral evolution as a 'default hypothesis' supported by citations to theoretical work. While this is a reasonable interpretation, it remains speculative without direct evidence of neutrality (e.g., population genetic data, fitness measurements). The proposal is appropriately framed as a hypothesis.

results.result: Complex transcription networks responsible for the same basic phenotype can undergo evolutionary changes much greater in magnitude than resulting phenotypic differences.
results.evaluation: Claim C127 summarizes the main conceptual finding of the study. This is well-supported by the comprehensive data showing extensive molecular changes (regulator requirements, target gene connections, gene expression) despite relatively similar biofilm phenotypes, particularly between C. albicans and C. dubliniensis.

results.result: Master transcription regulators controlling biofilm formation have undergone slow substitutions over evolutionary time, but their connections to target genes have changed rapidly.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12 summarize the main evolutionary finding from the abstract. This is well-supported by the comprehensive data showing gradual changes in regulator requirements (Figure 3) but rapid changes in regulator-target connections (Figure 4) and expression (Figure 5B), as quantified in Figure 6B.
